title: The Multifamily Market Is More Navigable Than the Headlines Suggest
summary: Explore multifamily market trends, easing supply pressure, agency capital updates, and regional growth.
body_markdown:
Over the past several weeks, I’ve had the opportunity to speak with borrowers, agency leaders, economists, investors, and owners across the multifamily industry. Those conversations have taken place in different settings, from a recent Lument webcast with leaders from Fannie Mae Multifamily and EBSCO Real Estate to client events and broader discussions about the economic outlook. In addition, my role as chair of Fannie Mae’s DUS Advisory Council has also provided opportunities to help shape the dialogue around borrowers’ needs and hear directly from Fannie Mae leadership and fellow lenders about the challenges and opportunities ahead. **


Many of the concerns across these conversations were remarkably similar. Interest rates, inflation, and the possibility of further market disruption remain significant sources of uncertainty.


Those concerns are understandable. The rate environment has become more challenging, and there is little evidence that a return to the low borrowing costs of the past decade is in the cards. But focusing solely on rates can obscure several developments that paint a more encouraging picture of the multifamily market today.


In my view, while the market has real challenges, it is proving more navigable than the top-line headlines suggest.


**Looking Beyond the Rate Story** Higher rates remain the most significant headwind facing the industry. Although the cost of capital has increased, many of the underlying fundamentals supporting multifamily performance are heading in the right direction. Occupancy has tightened, rent growth has improved modestly, and the labor market has remained healthy enough to support household formation and rental demand.


None of these trends eliminate the challenges associated with an acquisition or refinancing, but they do suggest a market that is adapting, albeit slowly, rather than stalling. For investors willing to look beyond short-term volatility, the gap between headlines and fundamentals is becoming increasingly important.


**The Supply Story Is Changing** One of the most significant developments in multifamily today is the shift in the supply outlook.


The industry is emerging from an unprecedented wave of new deliveries that placed pressure on rent growth across many markets. In numerous Sun Belt metros, heavy supply contributed to softer rents, higher concessions, and a more competitive leasing environment. Much of the hesitancy we have seen over the past two years can be traced to that surge in new inventory.


That dynamic is now beginning to change.


Construction starts have fallen significantly from their peak in 2022, and new deliveries are expected to moderate over the next several years. As supply pressure eases, market fundamentals, including concessions run-off, should continue to improve, particularly in markets where demand remained resilient throughout the cycle.


We are already seeing early signs of that transition. Rent growth, while still modest by historical standards, is moving in the right direction. The trend is not uniform across markets, but the broader supply-demand balance is becoming more favorable than it was even a year ago. For long-term investors, this trend matters.


**Capital Continues to Flow** Another misconception is that capital has disappeared from the market. It has not.


Lending activity has rebounded, investment sales volume has recovered from recent lows, and a broad range of capital sources continues to participate in multifamily finance. Agency lenders and banks remain the foundation of the market, while life companies, CMBS lenders, FHA, and other capital providers continue to contribute liquidity.


Just as importantly, lenders are adapting alongside borrowers. For instance, Fannie Mae recently introduced Streamlined Treasury Lock, designed to provide greater certainty earlier in the financing process. Freddie Mac’s new Optigo® Conventional Forward program is another example, giving developers greater confidence in the availability and terms of permanent financing before a project reaches stabilization. Together, these initiatives demonstrate how the industry can evolve in ways that help borrowers navigate volatility while supporting new multifamily development.


Capital may be more selective than it was during the peak years of the cycle, but it remains available for well-positioned borrowers and quality assets.


**Opportunity Favors Discipline** If there is a defining characteristic of today’s market, it is differentiation. Some markets are benefiting from limited new supply, improving occupancy, and rent growth that, while modest, is accelerating. Others are still working through excess inventory and elevated concessions. The days when markets moved in lockstep appear to be behind us. That is why disciplined market selection has become increasingly important.


Opportunity is already coming from a different mix of markets than those that led the last cycle. As investment in AI infrastructure and advanced technology continues to accelerate, several supply-constrained Bay Area markets, including San Francisco and San Jose, are posting the strongest rent growth in the country. At the same time, select Midwestern markets are gaining momentum, supported by limited new supply, relative affordability, and diversified employment bases that include manufacturing and logistics. These trends reinforce the importance of looking beyond broad national narratives and focusing on the local market fundamentals driving long-term performance.


Sophisticated investors remain active, particularly in markets where operating conditions are improving and new supply is tapering. As EBSCO’s Jimmy Adams noted during our recent webcast, patient capital can still find attractive investments in a higher-rate environment. Careful underwriting and a long-term view can provide a meaningful edge.


One observation I continue to come back to is that some of the strongest periods for real estate investing have occurred during higher-rate environments. That may seem counterintuitive given today’s focus on financing costs, but history suggests that elevated rates do not by themselves prevent strong returns. What matters is how markets adjust. The greatest challenge is often the period of transition, when values, financing structures, and investor expectations reset to a new environment. Once that adjustment occurs, disciplined investors are often well-positioned to capitalize on opportunities created by the preceding uncertainty.


**A More Constructive Outlook** The challenges facing multifamily are real. Interest rates remain elevated. Inflation remains a concern. Geopolitical and economic uncertainty continues to create volatility.


At the same time, supply is slowing, fundamentals are stabilizing and, in many cases, improving, capital remains available, and investors continue to find opportunities in select markets. Taken together, those trends point to a multifamily market that is gradually finding its footing.


The path forward may not be easy, but it is becoming clearer. For investors and owners willing to remain disciplined, prioritize sound underwriting, and take a long-term view, a challenging market can create attractive opportunities.
